transcript.text:
Greyhollow clings to the flank of the Stoneshell Mountains, a town of slate roofs and smoke cut into cold rock high above the timber line. For generations its folk have drawn iron and silver from the mountain, and the Temple of the Anvil Father, god of forge and fire, has watched over them from the upper end of the main street.

Brakka Ironvein served six years there as a temple guard: a steady dwarf with a smith's hands and a guard's watchfulness, until the town's quiet broke three days ago. Three miners went down into the old north workings, sealed a generation back, and none returned. Last night a fourth man staggered out of the dark alone, raving about lights that walked, and died before dawn.

At sunrise the town council means to brick the entrance shut, missing miners or not. The prior, old Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and he stands now at the mine mouth with a hooded lantern borrowed from the temple, the cold breath of the passage sighing out past him.

What do you do?

I check my gear first: lantern lit, weapon loose in its sheath, shield strapped tight. Then I crouch at the mine mouth and look for tracks or fresh marks in the dust and old seal timbers, to see how the three miners went in and whether anything came out.

You go through the old routine, patient as a temple guard: strap the shield tight, loosen the longsword in its scabbard, work the lantern's wick alight with your tinderbox until the flame catches and throws a warm circle out thirty feet, pale at the edges. The borrowed lantern was lent full, and it burns steady.

You crouch in the mouth of the passage and study the stone floor. The old seal is down: heavy timbers lie splintered just inside, pried and kicked aside. But the dust beyond them is a hopeless trampled mess, scuffed in every direction and drifted where the wind has breathed through. You can see that many feet and at least one body dragged over it in recent days, but the prints are all kicked over and blurred together. Try as you might, you can't pick out three men going in, or one man coming out, or anything else.

The passage beyond the broken seal slopes gently downward and out of the daylight, and the dark there is complete past your lantern's ring.

I give up on the tracks and ease past the splintered timbers, shield up and lantern held low in my left hand, going slowly down the slope. I keep my eyes on the walls and ceiling for old support beams, markings, or anything that glints, and listen for any sound beyond the wind.

You step over the splintered timbers and the mine closes around you, your lantern pushing back the dark as you go. The floor slopes steadily down, cut here and there into broad steps worn smooth by a generation of boots before the sealing. Old braces stand every few yards, thick with dust and green where water has run; most are sound, but here and there one leans, its wood soft with rot. The air turns still and cold and heavy, smelling of wet stone and old, sour decay. The sound of the wind dies away behind you until the only noise is the soft grit of your own boots.

After some minutes the slope levels out into a wide gallery, its roof lost above the lantern's reach. Here the dust is less trampled, and you find the first clear sign of the three men. A miner's pick is driven into a crack in the floor, its haft wrapped with a torn strip of shirt-cloth for a grip, and on the wall beside it a chalk arrow points back up the slope — the miners marking their way out. A little tin with a burnt candle-stub lies tipped near the pick, long cold.

You stop and listen. The mine is silent, the kind of silence that presses on the ears. Then, faint and far off, comes a soft scrape — stone on stone, or old timbers settling — and it is gone. Only the slow drip of water somewhere ahead remains.

I pick up the candle tin and examine the pick and the torn cloth, checking if the cloth is fresh and whether there's any blood or other marks. Then I look around the gallery for exits, noting which direction the scrape seemed to come from, and move toward it quietly with the lantern shuttered down to a narrow beam.

You turn the pick over in your hands. The haft's rag is torn linen shirtsleeve, stiff with coal dust and sweat, but not rotted — torn within the last few days, not a generation back. No blood on it. The pick's point carries bright fresh scratches where it bit rock recently. The candle-stub is burnt to a nub in a fresh little pool of wax, long cold, and there is no blood on that either. The three men were here whole and unharmed, and they left this as a waymark, plain as a signpost.

You lift the lantern and turn a slow circle. The gallery is a junction. Behind you, the entrance slope. Straight ahead, the main drift runs on, wide enough for two men abreast, with rusted rails laid for ore carts; a chalk arrow on the wall points down it. To either side, two narrower side drifts open into the dark, one half-choked with fallen rock. The scrape you heard seemed to come from the main drift, deeper in.

You shutter the lantern down to a narrow beam and go on, following the chalk arrow. But chain mail is a poor thing for silence: even moving slow and careful, the links chink faintly with each step, and your boots grate on the grit.

Some minutes down the drift, past more leaning timbers and the shine of water on the walls, you stop. Far ahead in the dark, beyond the reach of your beam, there is a light. A faint, pale yellow glow, low to the floor — and it sways, gently, the way a carried lantern sways in a walking hand. It holds for a long moment, then slides away and is gone around some bend, leaving the dark behind it.
Lights that walked, the fourth man said. I keep the beam narrow and move forward to the bend where the glow vanished, hugging the wall and stopping at the corner to listen before I look around it.

1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. story.text:
## The Story So Far

**Setting and setup.** Greyhollow is a mining town cut into the cold flank of the Stoneshell Mountains. The Temple of the Anvil Father — god of forge and fire — stands at the upper end of its main street. Brakka Ironvein, a hill dwarf fighter (level 1) and acolyte, served six years there as a temple guard.

Three days ago, three miners went down into the old north workings (a mine section sealed a generation ago) and none came back. Last night a fourth man staggered out alone, raving about "lights that walk," and died before dawn. The town council means to brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow. Prior Hessa, an old dwarf, asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

The game began late afternoon of Day 1, the 18th of Frost, 1174 (set at 4:30 PM), at the mine mouth, with a hooded lantern borrowed from the temple (lit, 6-hour oil timer). Brakka has darkvision 60 ft, AC 18 (chain mail + shield, disadvantage on Stealth), HP 14/14, 15 gp, and standard fighter gear.

## What Happened (turns 1–7)

**Turn 1.** Brakka lit the lantern and checked for tracks at the mine mouth; a Survival check rolled a 5 — too trampled to read. The old seal timbers lay splintered just inside.

**Turn 2.** He descended the slope (10 min) to a wide chamber I named **the first gallery**. Found a miner's pick driven into a floor crack (haft wrapped in torn shirt-cloth) and a chalk arrow on the wall pointing back up the slope — a waymark. Heard a faint, far-off scrape, then nothing.

**Turn 3.** Examining the pick/cloth/candle-stub (Perception 19): no blood, cloth torn within days, fresh bright scratches on the pick head — the miners were here unharmed, days ago. The gallery is a junction: the **main drift** (wide, with rusted ore-cart rails, chalk arrow pointing down it) continues ahead; two narrower side drifts, one half-collapsed. He moved quietly down the main drift (Stealth 9, chain mail disadvantage).

**Turn 4.** Far ahead he saw a faint pale-yellow light, low to the floor, swaying like a carried lantern, then it slid away around a bend.

**Turn 5.** Approached the bend (Perception 7, Stealth 3 — loud). Rounded the corner: 30 feet away stood a zombie miner carrying a lantern — a grey slack face, filmed eyes. Combat began. Initiative: Brakka 18, Zombie miner 5.

**Combat (rounds 1–3, turns 5–7).** The zombie (CR 1/4, AC 8, HP 22, Slam +3 for 1d6+1 bludgeoning, Undead Fortitude) never landed a hit — Brakka's AC 18 held. Brakka's longsword (+4, 1d8+4):
- Round 1: hit for 7 (22→15).
- Round 2: hit for 9 (15→6).
- Round 3: hit for 6 (6→0); Undead Fortitude CON save DC 11 succeeded (rolled 17), dropping it to 1 HP instead.

**Turn 8 (killed it, will be replayed).** Round 4: hit for 10 (1→0); Undead Fortitude save DC 15 failed (rolled 6). Zombie destroyed. Fight over after 4 rounds, +50 XP (now 50/300). Brakka took no damage the whole fight.

## Turns 8–12 (already happened; will be replayed word-for-word)

- **Turn 9:** Examined the dead miner: found a brass lamp tag stamped **OLIN** around his neck. No wound killed him — no blood, bones whole, but a grey livid stain spread over his chest over the heart, "like a bruise that never bled." Said a prayer over him.
- **Turn 10:** The dead man's lantern was still burning, nearly full of oil and freshly trimmed — lit only hours ago, not three days. Brakka took the tag (into his pouch) and the lantern (as a spare), and moved on.
- **Turn 11:** Found a fresh chalk arrow (drawn hours ago) pointing down a low side drift, with the word **ALIVE** scrawled beneath it. Entered and called out.
- **Turn 12:** Found **Ged Marrow**, a young survivor, holed up behind a timber-and-stone barricade in **the low drift**, ringed by many burning lamps and candle-stubs, a pick across his knees. He begs Brakka to keep the light burning.

## Where Things Stand (after turn 12)

- **Clock:** Day 1, 18th of Frost, 1174, about 5:00 PM. Sunrise deadline is Day 2 (19th of Frost).
- **Brakka:** HP 14/14, AC 18, XP 50/300, Second Wind unused, hit die 1/1. Items now include **Brass lamp tag (Olin's)** and a **Miner's lantern** (spare, nearly full of oil). Hooded lantern (borrowed) still burning with ~5.5 hours of oil left.
- **Location:** the low drift, at Ged's barricade.

## The Four Miners (established)

The crew who went down: **Olin** (found as a zombie, destroyed by Brakka — his tag taken), **Bram** (rose as a walking dead like Olin, still abroad in the mine — a live threat), **Ged Marrow** (alive, the survivor), and **Tobis** (the "fourth man" — fled the first night, reached the surface, died before dawn; Ged doesn't yet know he died).

## The Horror (what Ged told Brakka, turn 12)

Down in **the deep workings** — deeper galleries the miners "shouldn't have gone" — the **old dead** of a generation-ago disaster lie, and they rise when the light fails. The risen dead carry their own lamps, so a swaying light in the dark that seems friendly is actually one of the dead. Olin "went dark" first, then Bram. The dark does it. Keep the light burning, or they come.

## Open Threads and Plans

- **Quest "Bring back the miners":** get Ged (and any other living) out before sunrise, when the council bricks up the entrance.
- **Bram** is still out there as a walking dead — a likely obstacle on the way out.
- **The deep workings and the old dead** remain unexplored; the miners disturbed something down there.
- Brakka holds Olin's tag to return to his family, and will likely have to tell Ged that Tobis died.

## Decided but Not Yet Fully Revealed (keep consistent)

- **The grey livid stain over the heart** (no fatal wound, bloodless) is the signature of whatever killed the miners — a cold, life-draining touch from the deep. I have hinted at a shadow/specter-like drainer but have **not** decided its exact nature or stat block. It is meant to be a thing to flee/avoid (and keep light against), not necessarily a fight a lone level-1 fighter can win.
- **The generation-ago disaster** that killed the old shift and caused the sealing has not been given specific details yet (cave-in, gas, or something else). Keep it vague until revealed.
- **The light mechanic:** the risen dead come in the dark; light keeps them at bay (or at least lets one see them). The dead carry their lamps because holding a lamp is their last living instinct. This is Ged's account and belief, consistent so far.
- **The fourth man's fate above** (Tobis dying before dawn) was established in the opening; he is not down here. Whether anything follows from his death in town is an unexplored thread.
- Ged is weak (thirsty, sleepless, three days down) and terrified of the dark — getting him out will be the real challenge of the quest's end.

[The story so far: your own summary of turns 0 to 7, written when the conversation was cut short]
## The Story So Far

**Setting and setup.** Greyhollow is a mining town cut into the cold flank of the Stoneshell Mountains. The Temple of the Anvil Father — god of forge and fire — stands at the upper end of its main street. Brakka Ironvein, a hill dwarf fighter (level 1) and acolyte, served six years there as a temple guard.

Three days ago, three miners went down into the old north workings (a mine section sealed a generation ago) and none came back. Last night a fourth man staggered out alone, raving about "lights that walk," and died before dawn. The town council means to brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow. Prior Hessa, an old dwarf, asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

The game began late afternoon of Day 1, the 18th of Frost, 1174 (set at 4:30 PM), at the mine mouth, with a hooded lantern borrowed from the temple (lit, 6-hour oil timer). Brakka has darkvision 60 ft, AC 18 (chain mail + shield, disadvantage on Stealth), HP 14/14, 15 gp, and standard fighter gear.

## What Happened (turns 1–7)

**Turn 1.** Brakka lit the lantern and checked for tracks at the mine mouth; a Survival check rolled a 5 — too trampled to read. The old seal timbers lay splintered just inside.

**Turn 2.** He descended the slope (10 min) to a wide chamber I named **the first gallery**. Found a miner's pick driven into a floor crack (haft wrapped in torn shirt-cloth) and a chalk arrow on the wall pointing back up the slope — a waymark. Heard a faint, far-off scrape, then nothing.

**Turn 3.** Examining the pick/cloth/candle-stub (Perception 19): no blood, cloth torn within days, fresh bright scratches on the pick head — the miners were here unharmed, days ago. The gallery is a junction: the **main drift** (wide, with rusted ore-cart rails, chalk arrow pointing down it) continues ahead; two narrower side drifts, one half-collapsed. He moved quietly down the main drift (Stealth 9, chain mail disadvantage).

**Turn 4.** Far ahead he saw a faint pale-yellow light, low to the floor, swaying like a carried lantern, then it slid away around a bend.

**Turn 5.** Approached the bend (Perception 7, Stealth 3 — loud). Rounded the corner: 30 feet away stood a zombie miner carrying a lantern — a grey slack face, filmed eyes. Combat began. Initiative: Brakka 18, Zombie miner 5.

**Combat (rounds 1–3, turns 5–7).** The zombie (CR 1/4, AC 8, HP 22, Slam +3 for 1d6+1 bludgeoning, Undead Fortitude) never landed a hit — Brakka's AC 18 held. Brakka's longsword (+4, 1d8+4):
- Round 1: hit for 7 (22→15).
- Round 2: hit for 9 (15→6).
- Round 3: hit for 6 (6→0); Undead Fortitude CON save DC 11 succeeded (rolled 17), dropping it to 1 HP instead.

**Turn 8 (killed it, will be replayed).** Round 4: hit for 10 (1→0); Undead Fortitude save DC 15 failed (rolled 6). Zombie destroyed. Fight over after 4 rounds, +50 XP (now 50/300). Brakka took no damage the whole fight.

## Turns 8–12 (already happened; will be replayed word-for-word)

- **Turn 9:** Examined the dead miner: found a brass lamp tag stamped **OLIN** around his neck. No wound killed him — no blood, bones whole, but a grey livid stain spread over his chest over the heart, "like a bruise that never bled." Said a prayer over him.
- **Turn 10:** The dead man's lantern was still burning, nearly full of oil and freshly trimmed — lit only hours ago, not three days. Brakka took the tag (into his pouch) and the lantern (as a spare), and moved on.
- **Turn 11:** Found a fresh chalk arrow (drawn hours ago) pointing down a low side drift, with the word **ALIVE** scrawled beneath it. Entered and called out.
- **Turn 12:** Found **Ged Marrow**, a young survivor, holed up behind a timber-and-stone barricade in **the low drift**, ringed by many burning lamps and candle-stubs, a pick across his knees. He begs Brakka to keep the light burning.

## Where Things Stand (after turn 12)

- **Clock:** Day 1, 18th of Frost, 1174, about 5:00 PM. Sunrise deadline is Day 2 (19th of Frost).
- **Brakka:** HP 14/14, AC 18, XP 50/300, Second Wind unused, hit die 1/1. Items now include **Brass lamp tag (Olin's)** and a **Miner's lantern** (spare, nearly full of oil). Hooded lantern (borrowed) still burning with ~5.5 hours of oil left.
- **Location:** the low drift, at Ged's barricade.

## The Four Miners (established)

The crew who went down: **Olin** (found as a zombie, destroyed by Brakka — his tag taken), **Bram** (rose as a walking dead like Olin, still abroad in the mine — a live threat), **Ged Marrow** (alive, the survivor), and **Tobis** (the "fourth man" — fled the first night, reached the surface, died before dawn; Ged doesn't yet know he died).

## The Horror (what Ged told Brakka, turn 12)

Down in **the deep workings** — deeper galleries the miners "shouldn't have gone" — the **old dead** of a generation-ago disaster lie, and they rise when the light fails. The risen dead carry their own lamps, so a swaying light in the dark that seems friendly is actually one of the dead. Olin "went dark" first, then Bram. The dark does it. Keep the light burning, or they come.

## Open Threads and Plans

- **Quest "Bring back the miners":** get Ged (and any other living) out before sunrise, when the council bricks up the entrance.
- **Bram** is still out there as a walking dead — a likely obstacle on the way out.
- **The deep workings and the old dead** remain unexplored; the miners disturbed something down there.
- Brakka holds Olin's tag to return to his family, and will likely have to tell Ged that Tobis died.

## Decided but Not Yet Fully Revealed (keep consistent)

- **The grey livid stain over the heart** (no fatal wound, bloodless) is the signature of whatever killed the miners — a cold, life-draining touch from the deep. I have hinted at a shadow/specter-like drainer but have **not** decided its exact nature or stat block. It is meant to be a thing to flee/avoid (and keep light against), not necessarily a fight a lone level-1 fighter can win.
- **The generation-ago disaster** that killed the old shift and caused the sealing has not been given specific details yet (cave-in, gas, or something else). Keep it vague until revealed.
- **The light mechanic:** the risen dead come in the dark; light keeps them at bay (or at least lets one see them). The dead carry their lamps because holding a lamp is their last living instinct. This is Ged's account and belief, consistent so far.
- **The fourth man's fate above** (Tobis dying before dawn) was established in the opening; he is not down here. Whether anything follows from his death in town is an unexplored thread.
- Ged is weak (thirsty, sleepless, three days down) and terrified of the dark — getting him out will be the real challenge of the quest's end.

DM: You kneel and turn back the collar of his coat. Around his neck is a thin cord with a small brass tag, the kind the mine office stamps for the lamp tally. It reads: OLIN.

No wound killed this man. You go over him with a guard's care: his bones are whole, his coat marked only by coal dust and your own fresh cuts, and beneath those there is no older hurt — no pick wound, no crushed limb, no blood. Only this: across his chest, over the heart, a grey and livid stain has spread through the skin, like a bruise that never bled. You cannot say what made it.

You murmur the old words to the Anvil Father over him, and let him lie.

Then you take up his lantern. It still burns. You unscrew the cap and tilt it, and the flame gutters but holds. The oil is nearly full, and the wick is fresh-cut, burning clean. By its measure this lamp has not burned three days — it was lit only hours ago. And yet here it burns in a dead man's hand.

What do you do?

Turn 10:
Player: That lamp lit only hours ago bothers me: someone fed and trimmed it, and a dead man didn't do that. I tuck Olin's brass tag into my belt pouch to return to his family, clip the lantern to my belt as a spare, and move on down the drift with my own light narrowed, watching for whoever tended it.

DM: You leave Olin to his rest and go on, his lamp tag safe in your pouch and his lantern clipped at your belt — a spare with a clean wick and near-full oil. Your own light stays narrowed, a small grey pool in the dark.

The main drift runs on, its rails buckled here and there, and every so often a side drift opens like a black mouth, most of them fallen in and shored with old timber. The old chalk arrows, smeared and fading, mark the miners' way deeper. You go slowly, watching the dark ahead, but the mine gives you nothing — only the drip of water that echoes like a second set of feet, and shadows that seem to shift at the edge of your light.

Then, at a place where a low side drift branches off to the left, you stop. On the wall beside it is a chalk arrow, but not like the old ones. This one is white and sharp, drawn hours ago at most, and it points down the side drift. Beneath it, in the same shaking hand, is scrawled a single word: ALIVE.

The main drift runs on ahead, its rails leading deeper into the dark. The side drift is low and rough, shored with old timber, and the fresh arrow points down it.

What do you do?

Player: Alive. That's what Hessa sent me for. I duck into the low side drift, following the fresh arrow with my light narrowed, and call out in a low voice, "Brakka Ironvein, from the Temple of the Anvil Father. Anyone there?"

DM: You duck into the low drift. The roof is low enough that you must stoop, your helmet grazing the timber, and the passage is rough, its walls raw where the rock was cut and never smoothed. Your narrow light crawls along it.

You call out, and the close stone swallows your voice strangely. For a long moment there is only the drip of water. Then, from deeper in, around a bend, comes a scrape of movement — and a voice, thin and hoarse and trembling with hope:

"Here! Back here! By the Anvil, a dwarf — from the temple, you said? Keep your light up! Keep it burning, and come slow. Come slow, and don't let it go out."

You ease forward. Around the bend the drift opens a little, and there a rough barricade of timbers and fallen stone is built across the passage. Behind it a ring of small lamps and candle-stubs, every one of them burning, throws a warm wavering light. And huddled behind the barricade, a pick clutched across his knees, is a young man, gaunt and hollow-eyed and grey with dust, staring at you as though he does not quite believe you are real.

"They sent someone," he whispers. "They sent someone after all."

What do you do?

Turn 12:
Player: I stop at the barricade, lower my sword, and keep my voice calm. "I'm Brakka, sent by Prior Hessa. What's your name, lad, and are you hurt? Is it just you, or are Olin's other friends with you?" I hold up Olin's brass tag so he can see it, and keep my eyes on the shadows behind him.

When you nod, he lets out a long, shaking breath. "Good. Good. He's at rest, then." He scrubs a grey hand over his face. "My name's Ged. Ged Marrow. I'm not hurt, sir — not deep. Thirsty, mostly, and I've not slept. I've been drinking the drip off the timbers."

He glances past you into the dark, then leans close, his voice dropping low. "There were four of us went down. Me, Olin, Bram, and Tobis. Tobis, he bolted the first night — scrambled back up toward the light. Did he... is Tobis well?" He waits, and something in your face must answer him, because he closes his eyes a moment. "Ah. Well."

Then he goes on, the words tumbling out now that they've started. "Olin went dark first. Then Bram. The dark does it, Brakka. Down in the deep there's a place we shouldn't have gone — the old dead are down there, and they get up when the light fails. You've got to keep your lamp burning. If it goes out, they come. And they carry their own lamps, so you'll see a light swaying in the dark and think it's a friend. It's not. It never is."

1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. You step in behind your shield, the blade already singing, and take Bram across the neck. The blow nearly parts his head from his shoulders, and this time there is no strength in the body to hold. You stoop and turn it. The wick is fresh-trimmed and burning clean, the oil full, just as Olin's was, and the flame is steady and patient, the work of a careful hand.

There is no hand here to have done it. The lamps of the dead are lit from somewhere deeper, in the dark below.

The way up the drift stands open now, the rails running toward the first gallery and the slope to the air, and no light waits between you and it that you can see.
